title: Cursed Market (ตลาดวัตถุต้องสาป)
tagline: Hidden-information trading game for 2–4 players: server-authoritative seeded rules, per-seat views, replayable audits. LAN only.
summary: Cursed Market is a 2–4 player browser game in which players choose merchant doors, inspect and appraise objects whose value, authenticity and curses are hidden, then trade with merchants and each other. A Node server owns the seeded rules and sends each seat only its own view; every finished match exports an audit that must replay to the same result. The rules grew from 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-24. The repo's own caveat: technical evidence does not prove the game is fun. It runs locally or on a LAN.
stack: Node.js 22.12 or later (HTTP and WebSocket server, node:test runner)
Self-hosted Thai and display fonts (Noto Sans Thai, Noto Serif Thai, Cormorant Garamond, IM Fell English, Srisakdi)

Images were produced with a built-in image generator, run through Codex CLI for the stage plates, with prompts and hashes stored. Impeccable design passes and scans are cited in the validation records. 54 Trail learning notes record decisions and ruled-out options, and 26 carry a cost line of minutes and tokens. A handoff file is written for a continuing agent. PRODUCT.md says its numeric balance values are assistant-selected experiments, not human-validated. The repo documents verification: node:test suites, strict seeded replays, scripted socket runs and independent finish-review records (the reviewer is not identified in them). Those results are the repo's reports; this review re-ran none. AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md and .gemini/ are named in learning notes but are not tracked at the pinned commit, so they were not read.

narrative.problem:
The repo's PRODUCT.md frames the project as a test: whether appraising and accepting a risky artifact creates enough temptation, doubt, commitment and surprise that players ask for another run. The one piece of human feedback it records concerned the earlier auction prototype, reported as lifeless, repetitive, predictable and not fun; participant counts and ratings are unknown. The appraisal game was added beside that prototype, which stays as a separate legacy entry.

Players are appraisers who choose doors to merchants (Orc, Vampire, Autometa, Alien, Dark One and Beast in the README; eight portraits exist in the catalog), inspect goods, state a value, bargain, buy and trade with each other. Base value, authenticity and curses are hidden, so information is the central engineering problem: each seat must be able to act on what it has learned and must not be able to read what it has not. Credits and goods also change hands between players, so transfers have to survive retries and be reproducible.
narrative.approach:
Rules live in one module, src/game/appraisal/, that the server calls and clients never touch. A client sends an intention; the engine applies it to a copy of the state, records it in a command log and returns the new state, or throws. No clock and no ambient randomness enter the rules: every chance outcome is a labelled HMAC draw from the match seed, so a match is a seed, a config and a command list.

The project also treats its own history as part of the design. Rule changes are put behind config flags so that audits recorded earlier still replay under the rules they were played with, and each feature has a dated validation report that lists what was and was not checked.
narrative.architecture:
A Node HTTP and WebSocket server (src/server/app.ts) hosts rooms in memory. RoomLifecycle owns room codes, seats, seat tokens, readiness, phase deadlines and reconnection; AppraisalRoomService adds the game: it parses messages, applies actions as the authenticated seat, plays bot seats and broadcasts a separate view to each seat. The shared protocol in src/shared/appraisal-protocol.ts types a seat action as the engine action without a player id.

The rules engine is the 41 files of src/game/appraisal/: engine, views, audit and one file per system (theft, secure storage, seals, price integrity, brokerage, survival, events). A React client in src/appraisal-client/ renders the private view; the earlier auction kernel stays in src/game/, src/client/ and src/server/main.ts. src/simulation/ and src/playtest/ hold the bot policies, the replay command and the audit report.
narrative.implementation:
applyAppraisalAction rejects a malformed request, returns the stored state for a repeated request id, throws request-conflict if that id returns with a different payload and stale-encounter for an old encounter number. It then clones the state, applies the action, bumps a revision, appends the action to the command log and runs assertAppraisalInvariants. The invariants include a money check: bank, wallets and vaults must sum to the configured total plus recorded funding, and the ledger replayed from the starting balances must equal every balance.

Hidden truth is generated from labelled draws when merchant stock is created and reaches a seat only through its own knowledge record. appraisalViewFor sends other seats as credits, energy, score, flags, item count and life; the viewer's own record is the player minus ten named private fields. True values appear only in the Collector results. Subsystems follow the same pattern: a theft duel seals the merchant's hand when it starts and the view exposes only whether the seat must choose or has submitted; market conditions are matched only against facts the seat knows, so selling is not a free test.

Commerce rules are small functions on the same state. An appraiser is paid a one-time 10% commission, rounded down, and gains trust with that merchant up to 10; each trust level adds five points to the chance a below-reservation price is accepted; being caught underpricing costs trust. Later systems add vaults with 4% interest, secured loans with escrowed collateral, price audits against an immutable base, and a Collector who scores goods at the end. Replay restores the run from seed and config, re-applies the commands and requires the exported audit to be deeply equal.
narrative.outcome:
At the pinned commit (2026-10-24, 45 commits) the repo holds a playable prototype with a React client, bot seats, a replay command and a validation folder of 162 files. The figures below are the repo's reports, not re-run here. The README, dated 2026-10-14, lists 352 tests, 120 seeded replays and six LAN runs for rules v0.5. Later documents record 789 of 789 tests at commit 3b45081 on 2026-10-23 and, in a UI report the same day, 821 of 822 with one network assertion failing under full load and passing alone.

Those runs were synthetic: the 120 replays use four scripted bot policies that read only the per-seat view, and the six socket runs used scripted clients. The repo's only human feedback concerns the earlier auction loop, its playtest worksheet for the appraisal game is empty, and there is no public deployment.
narrative.lessons:
What the repo's records say is still open or was learned.

Learned, as recorded: a dated self-review on 2026-10-23 found three high-severity defects that the tests had not: an untimed duel could stall a room, loans left open at match end let a borrower keep principal and collateral, and the Collector deadline constant had no consumer. Each was fixed behind a config flag so old audits still replay; the same record notes that another behaviour change under the secureEconomy flag was not given a rule version. A 2026-10-14 UI pass found the browser client rejected every v0.5 room, so survival had only been exercised through socket scripts until then.

Open: no human session of the appraisal game; bots play none of the theft, vault, loan or seal actions, so simulation figures say nothing about them; a merchant's tell can be countered about 73.5% of the time in the review's trials; the vault can be used to avoid theft compensation; a seat's own view is built by removing fields, so a new private field would leak by default; the README is stale; keyboard, hover and live seal flows were not exercised in a browser.

claims.text: The repository has 45 commits, from 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-24, all with the author email phcaradanai@gmail.com.

The commit log shows the rules growing in steps: life, energy and Collector on 2026-10-14; trust, pulse shards and trade changes on 2026-10-16; core v0.6 rules on 2026-10-22; PvP theft penalties, sinner seals and vault interest on 2026-10-23; a cabinet UI merged from a branch named codex/cabinet-ux on 2026-10-24.

25 of the 45 commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming Claude: 19 name Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 6 name Claude Opus 5.5. A Trail learning note also records a preference as told to Claude in two earlier sessions.

A client message is typed as an action without a player id, the parser rejects any key outside an allowed list, and the room service adds the acting player from the authenticated seat before calling the engine. The README states the same rule.

applyAppraisalAction returns the stored state for a repeated request id, throws request-conflict if the id returns with a different payload, throws stale-encounter for an old encounter number, and works on a deep copy; each applied action bumps a revision and is appended to a command log.

After every action assertAppraisalInvariants checks that bank, wallet and vault credits sum to the configured starting total adjusted by recorded round-reward and item funding, and replays the ledger from the starting balances to compare with every balance, so credits cannot change without a ledger entry.
All chance in the rules is randomAt(seed, label): an HMAC-SHA256 of a text label keyed by the match seed. It keeps no state, so an outcome depends on its label, not on how many draws came before.

At the pinned commit no line in src/game or src/simulation contains Math.random, no line in src/game contains Date.now, and 87 lines in src/game/appraisal call randomAt(. A match seed is 32 random bytes drawn when the host starts the match.

An item's hidden truth is drawn from labelled randomAt calls when merchant stock is created: genuine with probability 0.75, cursed 0.35, certificate 0.65. A seat learns it only through public knowledge or its own knowledge record.

The room service builds a separate view for each connected seat with appraisalViewFor(game, seat.id). Other seats appear only as credits, energy, score, flags, item count and life; an item view carries what that seat has learned, and adds the true base value, authenticity and curse only at RESULTS for goods the Collector scored.

In survival mode the view withholds value-derived history and hidden accuracy until results; the 2026-10-14 report records an independent review finding on exactly this (F2) and a command-only regression test for it.

A seat's own record is built by cloning the player and removing ten named fields, not by listing allowed fields, although the comment above it says allowlist. The 2026-10-23 review flags that a new private field would be sent to the client by default; the code is unchanged at the pinned commit.

A theft duel seals the merchant's hand when it starts, the server picks the target good in a player duel instead of accepting an id, hands are cleared once both are revealed, and the view sent to a seat holds only whether it must choose and whether it has submitted.

One test serialises the theft view and asserts it holds no hands or item id before resolution; another runs the same seed and choices twice and requires identical state; a third shows the sealed hand is the same whatever the request id or the player's later choice.

marketConditionMatch is given only facts the seat already knows and returns unknown when a required fact is missing; the design notes add that an unaffordable sacrifice is refused the same way for matching and mismatching goods, so selling cannot be used as a free test of a hidden property.

When goods an appraiser priced are first sold by the merchant, the appraiser is paid once a base commission of 10% of the price rounded down, and gains one trust with that merchant, capped at 10; a commissionPaid flag stops resale between players from paying again.

Each trust level adds five percentage points to the chance a merchant accepts a price below its reservation; being caught underpricing loses one trust. The catch and the acceptance are labelled seeded draws, and the design notes call the numbers trial values.

The Dark Market budget is capped at half of the bank's free funds, except that if every drawn order is too dear it opens the cheapest one the free bank can still back. Each order reserves its full quota payout, and an invariant requires the bank to cover the market budget plus promised rewards.

The secure economy (2026-10-23) adds vaults with 4% interest paid from the bank, secured loans whose collateral moves to an escrow owner with value and deadline frozen at funding, price audits against an item's immutable base, and PvP theft penalties of a seal, a two-encounter cooldown and four 5% compensation instalments.

Prices a player sets are audited against the item's immutable base: from 150% of base the audit chance is 25%, from 200% it is 50%, from 250% it is 100%. A flagged item sells to the system for 0 until the owner passes a paid reappraisal within 10% of base.

When every player has zero life, or after encounter 15 in new matches, the Collector scores each seat as credits plus item values, then one percentage modifier: a fake keeps 25% of base, a curse keeps 75%, and goods another seat appraised score 15% more.

A match audit can be exported only once the match reaches RESULTS. Replay restores the run from seed and config, re-applies every recorded command including the advance steps, and requires the result to be deeply equal to the audit.
Timeout defaults are recorded as ordinary commands with a request id naming match, encounter, phase and seat, and the report analyser checks every recorded timeout against the replayed run.
Bot seats act through the same engine actions as people and decide from the per-seat view type; a rejected bot action falls back to ending the turn.

Rule changes are put behind config flags and restoreAppraisalRun takes the exact saved config, so an audit recorded before a rule existed replays under the old rules; new matches get the current set from DEFAULT_APPRAISAL_CONFIG. After one fix the repo stored legacy audit hashes and re-checked that replay gave the same hashes in both modes.

Each feature has a dated report in docs/validation/ that links its raw artifacts: test output, build output, JSON from scripted socket runs, seeded-run summaries and a source-hash manifest. At the pinned commit the folder holds 162 files.

The README status paragraph is dated 2026-10-14 and reports 352 tests, a build, 120 seeded replays and six LAN runs; the v0.5 validation report of that date lists 349 tests plus 27 focused ones, and the repo's 2026-10-23 review calls the README stale. These are the repo's reports, not re-run here.

Later figures in the repo's records, not re-run here: 789 of 789 full-suite tests at commit 3b45081 on 2026-10-23, and 821 of 822 in a UI report the same day, where one network assertion failed under full load and passed when rerun alone. The 488 in the source-count capture is a grep of test( and it( lines, not a test count.

The 120 seeded runs reported on 2026-10-14 used four scripted bot policies that read only the per-seat view, across 2, 3 and 4 seats and 10 seeds each; every run was strictly replayed, and the summary file stores humanFunValidated: false.

Six scripted socket runs (2, 3 and 4 seats, timed and untimed) completed with Collector scoring, strict replay and rematch; the run's own scope line says it covered no browser, image inspection or human or device playtest.

The server closes a socket that sends more than 100 messages in a 5-second window (code 4008) and caps a message at 4,096 bytes; the first scripted LAN bot run exceeded that guard, and the repo changed the script's pacing while preserving the server guard.

A dated self-review (2026-10-23) ranked ten findings; its first three were an untimed duel that could stall a room, loans left unsettled at match end, and a Collector deadline constant with no consumer. Commit 8cfc55c addressed them: at the pinned commit a 30-second duel clock runs in untimed rooms, loans are foreclosed at match end, and collectorDue reads the deadline.

A 2026-10-14 UI pass found that the browser client rejected every v0.5 room state through a rulesVersion check, so survival had only been exercised through socket scripts until then; a regression test was added.

No line in src/simulation names the theft, vault, loan, seal or criminal-notice actions (0 matches against 20 in src/game/appraisal), and the repo's records say bots do not use seals; simulation figures therefore do not measure the secure economy.

A merchant's duel hand is its preferred hand with probability 0.6; the repo's review recorded 294 wins in 400 trials for a player who always counters it, and lists this and the vault and compensation interactions as playtest risks, not bugs.

The README says the technical evidence does not prove the game is fun, that testing with people is still needed, and that there is no human fun, balance or final brand approval yet. PRODUCT.md records the earlier auction prototype's feedback as lifeless, repetitive, predictable and not fun.
PRODUCT.md calls the numeric balance assistant-selected experiments, not human-validated balance, and the core v0.6 source comment says the same of its numbers.

The playtest folder holds protocols and a v0.5 session worksheet whose fields are empty at the pinned commit; the 2026-10-14 report says the only supplied human enjoyment evidence still concerns the old auction loop.

The 2026-10-23 secure-economy report says the seal and compensation screens were checked by server-rendered markup tests only, a live multi-seat seal flow was not exercised in a browser, and keyboard and hover behaviour was not independently exercised. It also says its checks establish technical behaviour, not human enjoyment or economy balance.
The same report states that the secure-economy rule version was not bumped when behaviour changed, so audits recorded before the change would now replay differently.

Creating a run checks that there are 2 to 4 distinct player ids matching a restricted pattern (reserved names such as __proto__ are refused), that the seed is a string of at most 256 characters, and that the config is valid.
Rooms are held in server memory with no database, and the repo says they do not survive a server restart; PRODUCT.md lists public hosting among things not included.

Server and tests are TypeScript on Node 22.12 or later; npm test builds the server and runs the built-in node:test runner over the compiled files. Dependencies include React 19, Vite 7, ws and Three.js.

The repo's documents attribute rules to 'the user' and keep them apart from agent proposals: the review lists rules the user confirmed as not bugs, and the handoff tells the next agent not to turn unconfirmed proposals into rules.

The 52 newer item and merchant paintings were generated with the built-in ImageGen tool, one call per asset; 16 earlier paintings were kept, and their prompt file records the mode 'built-in image_gen generate'. Prompts, hashes and sizes are stored in generation-prompts.json.
The 2.5D scene plates were produced with Codex CLI's built-in image_gen run non-interactively; the manifest stores each prompt, reference image and source and delivery hash.

The three v0.4 concept images were generated with the built-in image_gen tool; the repo labels them direction exploration, not screenshots of a working game, and their numbers and English text as mockup values.

The seven screenshots here come from the repo's validation records of 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-23; four of those records say the capture used a fixture or synthetic state to show a case deterministically, and all predate the cabinet UI merged on 2026-10-24.

excerpts.title: Seeded draws: one labelled HMAC per outcome
excerpts.why: randomAt keeps no state. A draw is HMAC-SHA256 keyed by the match seed over a text label, so an outcome depends only on its label (for example an item id plus ":genuine"), not on how many draws came before. Revealing one outcome does not expose another.

excerpts.title: Authority boundary: guards before any rule runs
excerpts.why: The first lines are the boundary. A repeated request id returns the stored state, a changed payload is request-conflict, an old encounter number is rejected, and the phase decides which action families are allowed. The state is deep-cloned before any change, and an open theft duel locks the seat to submitting its hand.

excerpts.title: Money checked by derivation, not trust
excerpts.why: Bank, wallets and vaults must sum to the configured total plus recorded round funding; then the ledger is replayed from the starting balances and compared with every balance. A rule that creates or loses credits without a ledger entry makes the next action throw.

excerpts.title: Audit export only at RESULTS; replay must match
excerpts.why: exportAppraisalAudit refuses to run before RESULTS, so the seed and hidden state are not downloadable mid-match. replayAppraisalAudit rebuilds the run from seed and config, re-applies each command including advance, and requires the exported audit to be deeply equal to the one supplied.

excerpts.title: The server decides who is acting
excerpts.why: A message carries a match id and an action without a player id. The room service rejects a stale match, then calls the engine with playerId set to the authenticated seat. A seat that has confirmed the reveal can only repeat requests the engine already accepted.

excerpts.title: A view built field by field
excerpts.why: The comment states the rule: no merchant hand, no concealed target and no opposing hand reach a client. The seat gets only whether it needs to choose and whether it has submitted, plus rounds already revealed, its own compensation schedule and its own crime record.

excerpts.title: Market conditions without a price oracle
excerpts.why: The comment on line 6 states the design rule. A contract can mismatch only on a fact the seat already holds; with a required fact unknown the result is unknown, so offering to sell cannot reveal whether the item is genuine or cursed. Requirement, bonus and cost are rolled from labelled draws.

excerpts.title: Privacy and determinism asserted in tests
excerpts.why: Two styles in one place: a privacy test that serialises the view and searches it for forbidden keys, and a determinism test that runs the same seed and choices twice and compares whole states with assert.deepEqual. The fixture uses a fixed seed, secure-theft.

demo.note: Runs locally: the README gives npm ci, npm run build and npm start, and other machines on the same network join by room code. No public deployment is documented.

limitations: The README says technical evidence does not prove the game is fun; testing with people is still needed. PRODUCT.md calls the numeric balance assistant-selected experiments, not human-validated balance.
The only human feedback on file concerns the earlier auction prototype (lifeless, repetitive, predictable, not fun). The v0.5 session worksheet for the appraisal game is empty at the pinned commit.
No public deployment: the game runs locally or on a LAN, and rooms live in server memory and do not survive a restart.

Test, replay and LAN figures are the repo's reports; this review re-ran none. The README status is dated 2026-10-14 and the repo's own 2026-10-23 review calls it stale; later reports give 789 of 789 and 821 of 822 full-suite results. The 488 in the source-count capture counts test( and it( lines, not tests.
The 120 seeded runs and six socket runs used scripted bots and clients; the LAN run's own scope line says it involved no browser, image inspection or human or device playtest.
Bots take none of the theft, vault, loan, seal or criminal-notice actions (0 matching lines in src/simulation), so simulation figures do not measure the secure economy.
The secure-economy rule version was not bumped when behaviour changed, so audits recorded in that window would replay differently (the repo's validation note).
A seat's own view is built by removing ten named fields rather than listing allowed ones; a new private field would be sent by default (the repo's 2026-10-23 review, still true at the pinned commit).
Always countering a merchant's theft tell won 294 of 400 trials in the repo's review; the review lists that and the vault and compensation interactions as playtest risks.

Browser coverage is partial: keyboard and hover behaviour were not independently exercised, the seal and compensation screens were checked by server-rendered markup tests only, and the v0.5 report did no browser or accessibility QA.
Screenshots are from fixtures or validation sessions of 2026-10-14 to 2026-10-23 and predate the cabinet UI merged on 2026-10-24; several show throwaway room codes.
Numeric balance values in core v0.6 and the commerce rules are marked experimental or trial in the repo's own documents.
